college-observational-policy.description: Thirteen-turn observational policy lifecycle covering two approved analyses, an approved HTML report, and a derivative communication scope.

turns.label: Domain review and framing
turns.prompt: Use the causal-consultant skill. Start with domain review: I am studying whether higher instructional expenditure improves later college graduation rates using observational data on 777 US colleges, for state education boards considering funding policy. Frame the decision, the meanings of Expend, Grad.Rate, and Private status, plausible mechanisms, and domain assumptions before data audit or analysis design.

turns.label: Clarify the policy claim
turns.prompt: The policy question is whether a feasible increase in spending would improve graduation outcomes, not merely whether richer colleges have higher graduation rates. What intervention and claim would be defensible with observational institutional data?

turns.label: Introduce data
turns.prompt: Here is data.csv. Grad.Rate is the later outcome and Expend is the primary exposure. Inspect the data before proposing analysis.

turns.label: Audit causal readiness
turns.prompt: Audit the unit of observation, missingness, support, leakage, and variable timing. For this benchmark, treat Expend as measured before the later Grad.Rate outcome; check rather than assume the roles of the other variables.

turns.label: Check post-data causal readiness
turns.prompt: Using the domain review and completed data audit, assess causal and method readiness for the average effect of a feasible $1,000 increase in Expend on later Grad.Rate among represented colleges with adequate support. Identify the defensible adjustment logic, assumptions, and diagnostics, but do not prepare an approval-ready scope or execute analysis.

turns.label: Prepare first analysis scope
turns.prompt: Prepare an approval-ready first analysis scope for the average expenditure effect only. Do not execute it or create output yet.

turns.label: Approve first analysis
turns.prompt: I approve the exact analysis scope you just presented, including its claim boundary and diagnostics. Execute that scope without changes.

turns.label: Reassess heterogeneity support
turns.prompt: For this benchmark, treat a bounded exploratory association comparison of the Expend-Grad.Rate relationship by Private as useful even if causal effect modification is unsupported. Use one causal review operation to decide whether this target is mature enough for later scope review. Assess modifier timing and within-group Expend support from the completed audit and first-analysis evidence. If mature, establish the current design and support recommendation and non-causal claim boundary; otherwise record the smallest blocker. This is not the heterogeneity analysis: do not compute a new target estimate, contrast, interaction, or hypothesis test, and do not prepare or execute a scope.

turns.label: Prepare second analysis scope
turns.prompt: Using only the current design and support recommendation and non-causal claim boundary established in the prior turn, prepare one separate approval-ready analysis scope for the bounded exploratory association comparison by Private. Do not rerun causal review, execute analysis, or create output.

turns.label: Approve second analysis
turns.prompt: I approve the exact heterogeneity scope you just presented. Execute it without changes.

turns.label: Prepare report scope
turns.prompt: Prepare an HTML report scope using the two completed analyses, their existing evidence, and their limitations. Do not generate the report yet.

turns.label: Approve report
turns.prompt: I approve the exact HTML report scope just presented, including its evidence basis and claim boundary. Generate it without changing scope.

turns.label: Prepare derivative scope
turns.prompt: Prepare a three-section slide-style summary scope derived from the completed report. Treat it as derivative communication only, add no analysis, and do not generate a file until separately approved.

college-discovery-handoff.description: Eight-turn discovery-to-analysis workflow covering a bounded discovery artifact, independent causal review, exact analysis approval, and decision synthesis.

turns.label: Establish discovery context
turns.prompt: Use the causal-consultant skill. Start a discovery-led study of whether a feasible increase in Expend could improve later Grad.Rate in 777 colleges. For this benchmark, Private and Top10perc are baseline institutional attributes, Expend is measured before Grad.Rate, and the timing and causal roles of S.F.Ratio and other variables remain unresolved. Establish the construct meanings, plausible mechanisms, and temporal and background constraints only. Do not inspect data, run discovery, or choose an analysis method.

turns.label: Audit discovery inputs
turns.prompt: Here is data.csv. Audit the unit of observation, missingness, variable types, support around a feasible $1,000 Expend contrast, impossible outcome values, and which variables are suitable for a compact discovery exercise. Do not run discovery or causal review, prepare an analysis scope, estimate an effect, or create durable output.

turns.label: Scope bounded discovery
turns.prompt: Using the completed domain and data findings, scope one bounded causal-discovery exercise around Expend and later Grad.Rate. Name the exact method or method sequence, use a compact audited variable set, honor the fixed timing constraints, leave unresolved directions unoriented, and require a local adjacency or neighborhood result with stability or sensitivity diagnostics. Treat it as hypothesis generation only. Do not run it or create output yet.

turns.label: Run bounded discovery
turns.prompt: Run the exact bounded discovery scope you just presented without changing its target, inputs, variables, method plan, constraints, diagnostics, output type, or candidate-only claim boundary. Create exactly one durable discovery artifact containing the method and settings, candidate structure, stability evidence, and limitations. Do not select adjustment variables, choose the final causal method, estimate an effect, or call any edge a cause.

turns.label: Review discovery implications
turns.prompt: Use causal review to decide what the discovery artifact can and cannot change for the most defensible bounded question about a feasible $1,000 Expend increase and later Grad.Rate. Independently assess timing, adjustment validity, analysis readiness, design fit, and claim boundary; record one current design and any applicable support, or the smallest blocker. Treat any discovered edge or orientation as a candidate, not a causal fact or automatic adjustment rule. Do not rerun discovery, prepare an analysis scope, or estimate the target.

turns.label: Prepare bounded analysis scope
turns.prompt: Using only the current causal review, prepare one approval-ready analysis scope if it authorized a mature Expend-Grad.Rate question. Otherwise state the smallest blocker and do not invent a ready scope. Discovery may motivate diagnostics, but it must not determine adjustment or strengthen the claim. Do not rerun review, execute analysis, or create output.

turns.label: Approve bounded analysis
turns.prompt: I approve the exact current analysis scope, including its evidence basis, diagnostics, and claim boundary. Execute it without changes.

turns.label: Synthesize discovery and analysis
turns.prompt: Compare what the discovery artifact suggested with what the completed analysis can actually support for a state education board deciding whether to act now or invest in stronger longitudinal data. Separate hypothesis-generating structure from estimated evidence and remaining assumptions. Do not run new discovery or analysis, and do not create a report, artifact, or other output.

star-interference-saturation.description: Twelve-turn open STAR consultation for a novice education-board user, covering consultant-selected question and method choice, one approved analysis, one approved HTML report, and evidence-bound decision synthesis.

turns.label: Frame an open classroom decision
turns.prompt: Use the causal-consultant skill. I work with a state education board and know very little about causal inference. I have pupil-level data from Tennessee's Project STAR, and I want to know what this historical study can credibly tell us about kindergarten class arrangements and early test scores. Before seeing the file, frame the practical decision, the people affected, plausible class arrangements and outcomes, and the factual questions that must be resolved. Explain unfamiliar terms in ordinary language. Do not select a final target, causal claim, analysis method, or software, inspect data, prepare a scope, or run analysis.

turns.label: Explore and audit the STAR data
turns.prompt: Here is data.csv. Treat these study facts as fixed: each row represents a kindergarten pupil; pupils were randomly assigned within schools to small, regular, or regular-with-aide conditions; tmathssk and treadssk were measured after kindergarten assignment; and schidkn identifies the school. Audit what the file contains, including column meanings and coding, duplicate rows, missingness, arm sizes, school structure, outcome ranges, available identifiers, and the timing and possible roles of the remaining variables. State what the extract cannot reveal. Do not choose the final target or method, estimate an effect, or prepare or execute an analysis or report scope yet.

turns.label: Explain the study context
turns.prompt: Using the fixed study facts and completed audit, explain the education and trial context needed for a responsible analysis. Cover what the three class conditions mean, how random assignment helps and what it does not guarantee, plausible ways class arrangements could affect scores, the historical study population, and limits on applying the findings to schools today. Treat audited data facts as fixed and do not inspect the file again. Use plain language and define necessary technical terms. Do not choose the final question or method, prepare a scope, estimate an effect, or create output.

turns.label: Map questions the data could address
turns.prompt: Using the current data and domain findings, describe a small set of materially different questions that this file could answer, partially address, or only explore. For each, state in plain language what would be compared, which outcome and pupils it concerns, whether the evidence could be causal or only descriptive, the main assumption, and the school-board decision it could inform. If you need a decision from me, offer only choices that would materially change the question or workflow and recommend a sensible default. Do not make me choose an estimator or software package, select a final method, prepare a scope, execute analysis, or create output.

turns.label: Select the most useful direction
turns.prompt: I care more about a trustworthy and useful answer than about any particular treatment comparison or causal claim. Assess causal readiness and choose the single most defensible analysis question for this school-board decision. You may select any class-arrangement target, comparison, outcome, population, and causal or explicitly noncausal interpretation justified by the study. Explain why this question is more useful and credible than the alternatives in language I can understand. Recommend one analysis approach and any additional validity review it genuinely needs. Do not prepare an approval-ready scope, execute analysis, or create output.

turns.label: Stress-test and explain the recommendation
turns.prompt: Before scoping, stress-test the current recommendation against the study and data facts that could change it. Check whether the assignment and class coding are usable, outcomes were measured at the right time, missing data matter, pupils in the same school have related outcomes, examining many comparisons or outcomes could create chance findings, or variables measured after assignment are being used incorrectly. Also consider how much this historical Tennessee study can tell us about current schools. Revise the recommendation if needed. End with exactly one current recommendation and explain its comparison, outcome, population, what the analysis will estimate or summarize, strongest assumption, and what it would and would not establish. Do not prepare a scope, execute analysis, or create output.

turns.label: Prepare the consultant-selected analysis scope
turns.prompt: Prepare one approval-ready analysis scope, meaning the exact plan I would approve, for the single current recommendation. Make it precise about who is included, what class arrangement or exposure is compared with what, which outcome or outcomes are primary, what the analysis will estimate or summarize, how uncertainty and multiple comparisons or outcomes will be handled, required checks, output files, and what can and cannot be concluded. Choose the technical method, any additional validity review, and software internally, then explain those choices briefly in language I can understand. The scope may support a causal conclusion or an explicitly bounded noncausal conclusion, but it must be feasible and useful. Do not rerun data or causal review, execute the scope, generate a report, or create output.

turns.label: Approve the consultant-selected analysis
turns.prompt: I approve the exact current analysis scope you selected, including who and what it compares, its checks, outputs, and limits. Execute it without changes. If an unforeseen data or method condition prevents responsible completion, record valid infeasibility evidence for that same scope instead of substituting another analysis.

turns.label: Interpret the evidence for a novice
turns.prompt: I do not know causal inference. Explain what the completed analysis or infeasibility evidence actually says in ordinary language. If a numerical result was produced, explain its direction, size, uncertainty, comparison group, and population without relying on statistical significance alone. A colleague wants to say, 'Project STAR shows that our state should adopt the analyzed class arrangement now and should expect the same score change.' Explain whether the evidence supports that statement and why. Separate study facts, assumptions, results, and present-day policy limits. Do not calculate anything new, revise the approved scope, or create output.

turns.label: Prepare an evidence-bound HTML report scope
turns.prompt: Prepare one HTML decision-report scope for a school-board audience that knows little causal inference. Use only the completed analysis or its valid infeasibility evidence. Choose a clear structure, but require a plain-language question, the selected comparison and population, an accessible explanation of the approach, the checks and results or unmet requirement actually produced, uncertainty, limitations, what the board can and cannot conclude, and the most useful next evidence step. Bind every proposed claim, table, and figure to existing evidence. Do not run new analysis or generate the report yet.

turns.label: Approve the HTML report
turns.prompt: I approve the exact current HTML report scope. Generate it without changing the evidence basis, analysis status, or claim boundary. If the report cannot responsibly be completed, record valid infeasibility evidence for that same report scope instead of silently changing it.

turns.label: Synthesize the board decision
turns.prompt: Give the board a compact final recommendation using only the existing analysis and report evidence. Start with the decision implication, then summarize the main result or infeasibility finding, the most important uncertainty and present-day transport limit, one action the board can reasonably take now, and the single data or design improvement that would most improve the decision. Use plain language. Do not run more work, revise a scope, or create another artifact.

schooling-iv-late.description: Ten-turn instrumental-variable workflow covering domain and instrument review, one approved LATE analysis with optional statistical-validity support, an approved HTML report, and policy synthesis.

turns.label: Frame the instrument and decision
turns.prompt: Use the causal-consultant skill. I am studying the return to schooling for a policy team considering access to four-year colleges. In this 1976 cohort of young men, nearc4 records whether a four-year college was nearby in 1966, ed76 is later completed schooling, and lwage76 is later log hourly wage. Treat college proximity as a candidate instrument, not as automatically valid. Frame the decision, instrument, treatment, outcome, plausible pathways, local-effect target, and assumptions only. Do not inspect data, prepare a scope, or run analysis.

turns.label: Audit IV inputs
turns.prompt: Here is data.csv. Use data audit only to verify the unit, coding, missingness, support, derived fields, and timing of candidate covariates relative to nearc4, ed76, and lwage76. Pay particular attention to 1976 variables and education-derived experience. Do not run causal review, prepare a scope, estimate an effect, or create output.

turns.label: Review the schooling domain
turns.prompt: Use domain review only. Using the fixed study facts and completed data audit, review the education and labor-economics context needed to interpret nearc4, ed76, and lwage76: college proximity as a 1966 access proxy, meaningful schooling treatment versions, wage-outcome interpretation, the cohort and policy population, plausible pathways from proximity to wages other than schooling, and the policy meaning of a local complier effect. Clarify which audited variables are defensible pre-instrument covariates and which should be excluded or bounded because timing or coding remains uncertain. Treat audited data facts as fixed and do not inspect the data again. Do not run causal review, recommend an analysis design, prepare a scope, estimate an effect, or create output.

turns.label: Review IV readiness
turns.prompt: Use causal review, using the current data and domain reviews, to assess whether nearc4 can support an instrumental-variable analysis of ed76 on lwage76. Address relevance, timing, conditional independence, exclusion, monotonicity, treatment versions, the complier population, covariate timing, and weak-instrument inference. Treat first-stage strength as an execution diagnostic rather than a prerequisite to preparing its scope. Recommend `instrumental_variables` when the bounded analysis is mature enough for scope review; add `statistical-validity` support only if unresolved concerns exceed the IV route's normal diagnostics. Establish the current design and any justified support recommendation or the smallest remaining blocker. Do not prepare a scope or execute analysis.

turns.label: Prepare IV analysis scope
turns.prompt: Using only the current causal review, prepare one approval-ready IV scope for the local effect of ed76 on lwage76 using nearc4. Require a transparent analysis population, first stage, reduced form, 2SLS estimate, weak-instrument diagnostics or robust inference, pre-instrument balance evidence, an assumption table, and an explicit LATE boundary. Do not rerun review, execute analysis, or create output.

turns.label: Approve IV analysis
turns.prompt: I approve the exact current IV scope, including its diagnostic requirements and local-effect claim boundary. Execute it without changes.

turns.label: Test the LATE boundary
turns.prompt: A policymaker wants to quote the result as the average return to one more year of schooling for all workers. Explain whether the approved operation evidence permits that interpretation and what population and assumptions actually bound it. Do not run another model, revise the scope, or create output.

turns.label: Prepare IV report scope
turns.prompt: Prepare an HTML policy-report scope using only the approved operation evidence and its limitations. Require an honest evidence trace, including the diagnostics and estimates actually produced or any infeasibility finding, assumption status, complier interpretation, and policy boundary. Do not generate the report yet.

turns.label: Approve IV report
turns.prompt: I approve the exact current HTML report scope. Generate it from the approved operation evidence without turning a local estimate into a population ATE or treating diagnostics as proof of instrument validity.

turns.label: Synthesize the access-policy decision
turns.prompt: Give the policy team a compact recommendation based only on the existing operation and report evidence, distinguishing what the evidence supports from what still depends on exclusion, monotonicity, and transport beyond compliers. Do not run more analysis, revise a scope, or create another artifact.
